fit: fresh or harvest-period fig exposure and an attributed intoxication metaphor
assessment: The travel account reports an impression of greater excitement during the harvest and a local saying. It does not identify a dated eater, fermented preparation, measured alcohol, Parkinson disease or visual disturbance.

fit: fresh figs and literary description of harvest excitement
assessment: The account explicitly names fresh figs and uses an intoxication metaphor. Independence from earlier travel literature is uncertain. The phrasing provides no clinical episode measurement.

fit: mixed dried sweet fruit category in author observations
assessment: Dried figs appear in a pooled row listing cognitive complaints, without item-specific observation counts. Hallucinations are named in other rows. No dried-fig visual episode or Parkinson diagnosis is established.

fit: oral fruit extract and rat drug-challenge task timings
assessment: The larger fruit-extract group shows shorter reward-chamber and transfer latencies than scopolamine alone. The smaller group contrasts are inconclusive. The test uses a fruit extract and maze proxies, with no clinical visual episodes.

fit: clinical fig allergy and dried-fig extract cross-reactivity
assessment: Five patients had allergic symptoms after fig ingestion. The laboratory separates fresh and dried extract inhibition. Reported percentages reflect IgE binding, with no hallucination outcome or preparation-specific clinical rate.

fit: fig leaf extract and behavior after acute or chronic stress in rats
assessment: The original figures distinguish lower anxiety-like behavior during chronic stress, better acute recognition task performance, and inconclusive acute immobility. They do not measure a visual episode or dried fruit effect.

fit: stem-bark extract and its fraction in nonclinical convulsion experiments
assessment: The original body confirms stem bark. Outcomes concern provoked convulsions and righting reflex, while a separate central assay examines glycine-related effects. No culinary fruit or human Parkinson outcomes are tested.

fit: fig peel cultivar extracts in a nematode amyloid model
assessment: Original abstract reports less paralysis and amyloid aggregation with Peggy Red peel extract. Full outcome tables remain restricted. The model does not measure human hallucination frequency.

fit: assigned medication and visual hallucination adverse event counts
assessment: Across two pooled Parkinson trials, 18/100 on extended-release amantadine and 3/98 on placebo reported visual hallucinations. These counts are incidence and time to first event under a medication comparison and do not estimate episodes per patient or fig effects.

fit: feeling of presence and first visual hallucinations in a Parkinson follow-up
assessment: The 78-person follow-up records 17 new feelings of presence and 26 people with newly reported visual hallucinations. First onset and preceding presence are distinct from episode frequency under a food exposure.
